title: Once in a thousand years
hookLine: if the stars came once in a thousand years we'd adore them; they come every night
carry: wonder is owed to what comes every night

cards: A grocery store parking lot after dark. Someone is loading bags into a trunk, checking the receipt, finding the keys. Above them, the whole sky is doing what it does every clear night.
They don't look up. Nobody would blame them; it's always there. That's exactly the trouble Emerson puts his finger on, a few lines after he sends his reader out under the stars.
What if the sky weren't always there? You met his answer back on day nineteen; today, a closer look.

teach.h: ONE NIGHT IN A THOUSAND YEARS.
teach.b: First, the line itself. "If the stars should appear one night in a thousand years, how would men believe and adore; and preserve for many generations the remembrance of the city of God which had been shown!"
Crowds on every roof. Stories handed down to grandchildren. A night people would date their lives by.
Second, the turn. "But every night come out these envoys of beauty, and light the universe with their admonishing smile." Envoys: messengers sent with something to deliver.
Because they come every night, we stop answering the door. Third, that odd word, admonishing.
An admonishing smile is one that also corrects you, kindly. The stars aren't scolding, but their steady return is a quiet reminder of what we've stopped noticing.
Emerson goes on to say they stir a kind of reverence because they're always present and yet out of reach. Fourth, between one breakfast and the next.

The trouble isn't that wonder is rare. It's that the things worth wonder are common, and so they become furniture: a face you see every morning, the fact that water comes out of a tap, rain on a roof.
Emerson isn't asking for new sights. He's asking for new eyes on the old ones. The envoys keep coming whether anyone answers.
The practice is simply to answer once.

how: Readers of Emerson sometimes use this passage from Nature as a prompt for looking at familiar things, a night sky, a face, a street, as if seeing them for the first time.

games.q: what does “once in a thousand years” mean?
o: a rare sight we'd adore, yet the stars come every night
a comet Emerson saw once and wrote about in awe
an old saying that great people are born rarely

games.q: inside once in a thousand years: tap the pairs.
p: one night in a thousand years
how people would believe and adore

s: Emerson says the stars come out rarely, so we should treasure them
his point is the opposite: they come out every night, and that's why we stop looking.
he calls the stars envoys of beauty
messengers who come every night with an admonishing smile.
an admonishing smile corrects you, but it is still a smile.

games.q: the stars appear only one night in a thousand years, and tonight is the night. what does Emerson say people would do?
o: believe and adore, and remember it for generations.
argue about whether it was real.
games.why: "how would men believe and adore" — and then he turns: they come out every night.

practice: Choose one ordinary thing in sight, your hand, a cup, a window, a plant, and look at it as though it appears only once in a thousand years, and this is the night. Notice its color, its edges, how the light sits on it.
When your mind says I know what that is, look again anyway, and let it be strange for a moment.

wordCard.voice: Once in a thousand years. Emerson's thought that if the stars came out that rarely, people would believe and adore, and yet they come out every night. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: wonder is owed to what comes every night. The face you see every morning counts too. See you tomorrow.
